Work out that $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ has mass 43 and $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$ also has mass 43, then check which molecules can form them.

walkthrough:
**Recall what a fragment peak means**

A peak at m/e = 43 means a positively charged fragment with relative mass 43 is formed. Let's look for combinations that add to 43.

$$M_r(\text{fragment}) = 43$$

**Spot two common fragments with mass 43**

Two very common fragments both weigh 43. The acylium ion and the propyl ion.

$$M_r(\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+) = 12 + 3 + 12 + 16 = 43$$
$$M_r(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+) = (3 \times 12) + (7 \times 1) = 43$$

**Check ethanal, compound 1**

Ethanal is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ with $M_r = 44$. Losing the aldehydic H gives the stable $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ ion.

$$[\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}]^+ \rightarrow [\text{CH}_3\text{CO}]^+ + \text{H}^\cdot$$
So compound 1 gives m/e = 43.

**Check both propanols, compounds 2 and 3**

Both propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$ with $M_r = 60$. Losing an OH group leaves the $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$ ion.

$$[\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{OH}]^+ \rightarrow [\text{C}_3\text{H}_7]^+ + \cdot\text{OH}$$
$$60 - 17 = 43$$
So compounds 2 and 3 also give m/e = 43, meaning all three do.

options.A: This says only ethanal gives 43 via CH3CO+. That part is true, but it misses that both propanols can also give 43 via C3H7+ by loss of OH, so it is incomplete.
options.B: This correctly includes ethanal and propan-1-ol but wrongly leaves out propan-2-ol. Both propanol isomers have the same Mr of 60 and both can lose OH to form C3H7+ at m/e = 43.
options.C: This correctly includes both propanols but wrongly leaves out ethanal. Ethanal readily loses its aldehyde H to form the very stable CH3CO+ ion at m/e = 43.
options.D: All three give m/e = 43. Ethanal forms CH3CO+ (44 - 1), while propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol both form C3H7+ (60 - 17). This matches the observed fragment in each spectrum.
